URACISME: Faire le pied de grue pour des: URACISME: Camping Out for Structural Change
Après de nombreuses pressions exercées p: After sustained pressure from a student collective, the president's committee for a racism-free campus was formed.
Pendant six jours, des étudiants de l’Un: For six days, University of Ottawa students camped outside the office of their president, Jacques Frémont. From Friday to last Wednesday, for 120 hours, they picketed to demand structural changes to fight racism on their campus. They specifically asked for a dialogue with the president and the vice-president, Jill Scott. But the meeting never took place.
À la suite de conversations en boucle pe: After a full year of conversations going in circles, the President's Advisory Committee for a Racism-Free Campus was dissolved on November 23, some time after <l1>the N-word controversy</l1>. The University of Ottawa is now proposing an Anti-Racism and Inclusion Action Committee, <l2>whose special advisor is Boulou Ebanda de B’béri. </l2>The new committee has drawn anger from students and some professors.
Ceux-ci estiment que le précédent comité: They believe the previous committee had made concrete proposals that the university administration never implemented. La Converse went to meet the protesters to understand what lies behind this affair, which reveals a trend in Canadian universities.
<strong>« Je rate une leçon pour vous en: “I’m missing a class to teach you one”
Installés sur de petits bancs de cuir, p: Seated on small leather benches and wearing masks, more than thirty of them are waiting it out in a room. The president's office is in this building. Posters with the hashtag #URACISME are plastered everywhere. “I’m missing a class to teach you one and I’m fed up with being silenced,” reads a protest sign placed near the president's office. Not far from it hangs a painted portrait of Mr. Frémont on a gigantic canvas as tall as the wall. Judy El-Mohtadi did not expect to stay this long.
« On pensait que le recteur allait accep: “We thought the president would agree to see us after a few hours; we were only asking for a dialogue. It’s as if we didn’t have enough legitimacy in the university’s eyes. It’s very condescending,” she says at the end of this six-day demonstration. The students oppose the creation of a second committee against racism and are demanding that the recommendations issued by the first committee be implemented. During the peaceful protest, two white men in their forties entered the building and hurled antisemitic insults and abuse at the students.
L’un deux était vêtu d’un uniforme milit: One of them was wearing a military uniform. “You’re Jews, you’re communists, you want to divide us,” they shouted, among other things. The scene shook the young protesters. “What stayed with me was the military outfit one of them was wearing,” says Khadija El Hilali, who was the first to see the men enter the building through the lower stairs.
« Nous avons réussi à calmer la situatio: “We managed to calm the situation without calling Protection Services,” the student adds. That same evening, members of the Gee Gees, the university’s varsity teams, came to sleep alongside the protesters to ensure their safety. “This kind of intimidation isn’t new to us; it happens often since we started speaking out on racial issues,” Khadija explains. According to Babacar Faye, president of the Student Federation of the University of Ottawa, who was also at the sit-in, the current climate is very difficult for Black students.
Après le débat entourant l’utilisation d: After the debate over the use of the N-word in classes, the N-word was spray-painted on a faculty member’s door and on a car parked near campus. White supremacist messages were sent to a printer, which kept printing them until it was unplugged. “It seems like the university doesn’t see what’s going on and doesn’t understand that the situation is particularly hard for Black students. I get messages from international students telling me they face discrimination as soon as they arrive at the university, or when they need support,” he says.
« La façon dont l’université a traité le: “The way the university has handled the problem is by pretending there are measures when there aren’t any. It’s simply a re-branding. In reality, nobody consults the students. It looks more like a media effort than an effort to fight anti-Black racism,” Babacar continues. Yanaminah Thullah, co-president of the Association des Leaders Étudiants Noirs, also picketed outside the president's office. For her, this story goes beyond what is happening at the University of Ottawa.
« C’est important pour moi d’être ici, c: “It’s important for me to be here because, as a Black woman, this is a battle I have to fight whether I want to or not. It’s a fight that goes beyond me, and it doesn’t concern only Black students. I’m also fighting for Indigenous students and other racialized students who are treated differently on campus. In short, it’s a battle for the community and against systemic racism.”
«Nous ne voulons pas dire à l’administra: “We don’t want to tell the administration what to do; we only want the university to understand how it is hurting us and how it can avoid hurting us,” adds Yanaminah, who believes the university reacted quickly by putting measures in place to fight racism, but that they proved to have no long-term effect. “It won’t happen in a day; these are small changes, but they can take us far,” the student concludes.
Tout a commencé avec l’interpellation de: It all started with the stop of Jamal Koulmiye-Boyce. In June 2019, the 20-year-old student, then vice-president of the Conflict Studies and Human Rights Students' Association, went to his office on campus. A security guard stopped him and asked for his ID, which the young man did not have on him. “I was told I didn’t look like a student and that this wasn’t a place for me. I took out my phone and started filming the scene while explaining that I didn’t feel comfortable,” he says. Jamal ended up handcuffed for more than two hours, surrounded by five campus security guards. Ottawa police officers then intervened.
« J’étais sous le choc, je leur ai deman: “I was in shock. I asked them why I was handcuffed and why the police had been called. The officers put me in the back of a patrol car. I asked them to take the handcuffs off and they told me to shut up, that they had a gun and that I could end up in jail. Afterwards, they took the handcuffs off and said to me: ‘I hope you’ve learned your lesson.’ And they left.”
Deux ans plus tôt, lors de sa semaine d’: Two years earlier, during his orientation week, he had been unable to take part in an evening event because he didn’t have his T-shirt. A police officer had stepped in, cut his wristband and dragged him off campus. Jamal was 18 at the time. For him, these two incidents reveal a problem of racial profiling on campus, and he wants it to stop. After the second incident, he posted a series of tweets and the blunder was covered by numerous media outlets, which embarrassed the university.
Après de nombreuses pressions exercées p: After sustained pressure from a student collective, the president's committee for a racism-free campus was formed. “At first, this committee was made up of university staff, and very few racialized people sat on it. We prepared a press conference to denounce the university’s inaction.
Après cela, quelques heures avant de la: After that, a few hours before the committee’s first meeting, we were invited to take part,” the student recounts. He was also at the sit-in, and says he spent an exhausting year.
« J’ai des frères plus jeunes, et quand: “I have younger brothers, and when they go to university, as Black students, they shouldn’t have to make sure their safety is guaranteed when they’re there to get an education. That’s why we’re holding this sit-in: we’re fed up with this succession of incidents and committees.”
<strong>Les comités : « un cycle dangere: The committees: “a dangerous cycle with no tangible change”
Pendant plus d’un an, étudiants et profe: For more than a year, students and professors worked together on the first committee – created following the discrimination denounced by Jamal Koulmiye-Boyce – to develop recommendations. The committee was chosen by the president and its mandate was to advise him. Jason Seguya, equity commissioner with the Student Federation of the University of Ottawa, sat on the dissolved committee. The fourth-year student, who took part in the recent sit-in outside the president's office, notes that the university tends to avoid structural changes.
« On a fait nos recherches sur ce qui se: “We researched what’s being done at other universities, and we proposed concrete recommendations against racism. We quickly discovered that other collectives had, in previous years, proposed recommendations along the same lines as ours, but they were never implemented.
Il est donc devenu clair pour nous qu’on: So it became clear to us that we were getting into a very dangerous cycle,” he says. For a year, with about ten racialized students and the collaboration of the Racialized Faculty and Librarians Caucus, the committee proposed structural changes against racism to President Jacques Frémont.
Magalie Lefèbvre, commissaire à l’équité: Magalie Lefèbvre, equity commissioner with the Graduate Students' Association of the University of Ottawa (GSAÉD), also sat on this committee. According to her, the president rarely came to the meetings.
Une information que confirment d’autres: Other committee members confirm this. She also believes racialized students were instrumentalized on the first committee. Professor Nadia Abu-Zahra, of the Racialized Faculty and Librarians Caucus, also sat on the committee. “When we realized that the new security advisor, <l1>Dan Delaney</l1>, was an Ottawa police superintendent who had previously killed an Indigenous person in crisis, the university didn’t want to talk about it,” she says.
«Lors de la dernière rencontre du 21 oct: “At the last meeting, on October 21, we expressed reservations about the fact that the committee was only making recommendations. We said we needed an action committee, that we couldn’t simply advise the president,” says Nadia Abu-Zahra. At the president's request, a few days later the caucus made recommendations for an anti-racist university in a report titled “L’université de demain”.
Les mesures proposées par les professeur: The measures proposed by the professors and the students were very similar. Six days later, the committee was dissolved, the recommendations were ignored and the president proposed a new committee. For his part, Jacques Frémont declined our interview request. But according to the communications office, he is listening to the university community and acting in consultation with it. “An action plan without adequate input from the community is doomed to fail. For more than a year, we have been listening to these students, as well as many other Black, Indigenous and racialized people, members of the student body, the faculty or the staff – and we will continue to do so. […] The president believes we must act quickly.
Nous respectons le droit des étudiants d: We respect students’ right to express their views on such a crucial issue and we denounce racism in all its forms,” was all Isabelle Mailloux-Pulkinghorn, media relations manager at the University of Ottawa, would say in response.
Jason Seguya, commissaire à l’équité aup: Jason Seguya, equity commissioner with the Student Federation of the University of Ottawa, sat on the dissolved committee. Photo: Lela Savic
Mais comment créer une université anti-r: But how do you create an anti-racist university? “Our demands are already being implemented at other universities,” points out student Jason Seguya. The students and professors specifically recommend a mandatory course on anti-racism. Khadija El Hilali has in fact launched <l1>a petition in favour of such a course for all students at Carleton University and the University of Ottawa</l1>.
« Du côté de Carleton, l’université est: “At Carleton, the university supports the initiative […] but at the University of Ottawa, it took more than two months to get a response from the president,” says the founder of the campus anti-racist collective. The recommendations report L’Université de demain also proposes creating an anti-racism office, as at the University of Toronto.
Ce bureau serait doté de ressources adéq: This office would be equipped with adequate resources to help resolve complaints, develop an educational program on anti-racism, guide strategic initiatives for anti-racist and decolonial education, and ensure community awareness and engagement. It would also be independent of the president. The students also propose better funding for student organizations and a centre for Indigenous and Black experiences.
« On ne devrait pas avoir à faire ce tra: “We shouldn’t have to be doing this work during our exams, and in the middle of a pandemic,” says Jamal Koulmiye-Boyce indignantly. “It’s a task that should be paid, with adequate resources.” In line with <l1>the wellness services at Queen’s University</l1>, the report L’université de demain proposes hiring mental health clinicians specialized in trauma caused by experiences of racialization. The therapists should be diverse enough for clients to be able to choose someone from their own ethnic group.
Ils devraient également être en mesure d: They should also be able to demonstrate their experience and success in helping racialized people who must cope with the stress and trauma caused by racism, colonialism and discrimination.
<strong>Des échos bien au-delà de l’Univ: Echoes far beyond the University of Ottawa
Mais cette affaire va au-delà de l’Unive: But this affair goes beyond the University of Ottawa. It can in fact be traced back to retired Canadian senator Anne Cools and an incident she experienced in the 1960s. “This situation reminds me a lot of what we went through in<l1> 1969 at Concordia</l1>, which was then called Sir George Williams University,” says Ms. Cools.
Un groupe d’étudiants de Concordia avait: A group of Concordia students had organized a<l1> 10-day sit-in</l1> on the ninth floor of the building, after a controversy with a biology professor, Peter Anderson. He allegedly graded Black students from the Caribbean lower than white students and, generally, treated them differently.
Après des manifestations, le professeur: After protests, the professor stopped teaching, and the university offered to create a committee to investigate the students’ complaints. The students called the proposal a “kangaroo court.”
« C’était absurde. Nous étions diffamés,: “It was absurd. We were being slandered; the university didn’t understand what the Black students were going through,” says the senator, who was among the protesters. Ms. Cools was arrested and imprisoned for a few months. Several students were even deported.
Aujourd’hui, elle estime que les comités: Today, she believes committees can be useful if you’re working with honest people. “But you constantly have to support them,” the former senator specifies.
« Une fois qu’on rentre dans le langage: “Once you enter the language of committees, you’re dealing with very serious laws. Because they create circumstances that exclude us, without our thinking we’re being excluded. It’s absurd. So if we can avoid them and rely on morality and principles, I think we have a better chance of succeeding,” she says bluntly.
Pour ce qui est de la situation qui prév: As for the situation at the University of Ottawa, Ms. Cools says she would like to have a conversation with President Jacques Frémont. “He would be a little more aware of his position and more careful about his actions.”
Quant aux étudiants, elle leur suggère d: As for the students, she suggests they learn what people can do to protect their interests. “It’s better to learn how power operates when you’re young than to discover it later and be terribly disappointed as you grow older.”
